NOTE 30

This note contains the proof that forms 14 (The Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem), [14 BM], [14 BN], and [14 BO] are equivalent. ([14 BM]: A system of equations over a finite ring $R$ has a solution in $R$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $R$. [14 BN]: A system of equations over a finite field $F$ has a solution in $F$ if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $F$. [14 BO]: A system of equations over a finite structure $(A,\,+,\,\cdot )$ has a solution in $A$, if and only if every finite sub-system has a solution in $A$.) First, it is clear that [14 BO] implies [14 BM] implies [14 BN]. We shall show that [14 J] implies [14 BO] and that [14 BN] implies 14.

NOTE 31

Definitions for forms [14 W], [70 A], [52 H] through [52 L], 372 and [372 A] through [372 D]. These are modifications of definitions from Schechter [1996a] and [1996b].

1.

A pre-order is a reflexive, transitive relation.

2.

A directed set $(\mathbb{D},\,\leq )$ is a non-empty, preordered set in which each finite subset has an upper bound.

3.

A net in a set $X$ is any function from a directed set into $X$. $(x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X$, usually denoted $(x(\delta ):\delta \in \mathbb{D})$ or $(x_{\delta }))$.

4.

If $x:\mathbb{D}\rightarrow X$ is a net and $S$ is any set we say $x$ is eventually in $S$ if $(\exists \delta _{o}\in \mathbb{D})(\forall \delta \in \mathbb{D})(\delta \geq \delta _{o}\rightarrow x(\delta )\in S)$ and we say $x$ is frequently in $S$ if $(\forall \delta \in \mathbb{D})(\exists \delta ^{\prime }\in \mathbb{D})(\delta ^{\prime }\geq \delta$ and $x(\delta ^{\prime })\in S)$

5.

$x$ is frequently constant if for some $c,\,x$ is frequently in $\{c\}$.

6.

Assume $(x(\alpha ):\alpha \in \mathbb{A})$ and $(y(\beta ):\beta \in \mathbb{B})$ are two nets in $X$, then $(y(\beta ))$ is a subnet of $(x(\alpha ))$ (in the sense of Aarnes and Andenees - (This is not the usual definition of subnet.)) if $(\forall S\subseteq X)$(If ($x(\alpha ))$ is eventually in $S$, then $(y(\beta ))$ is eventually in $S$). (Which is equivalent to $(\forall S\subseteq X)($ If $(y(\beta ))$ is frequently in $S$ then $(x(\alpha ))$ is frequently in $S$). )

7.

A universal net (or ultranet) on a set $X$ is a net $(x(\delta ):\delta \in \mathbb{D})$ with the property that $(\forall S\subseteq X)$ ($x$ is eventually in $S$ or $x$ is eventually in $X\backslash S$).

8.

A partially ordered set is Dedekind complete if each subset that has an upper bound has a least upper bound. (Equivalently, if each subset that has a lower bound has a greatest lower bound.)

9.

An ordered vector space is a real vector space $Z$ equipped with a partial ordering $\preccurlyeq$ which also satisfies:

$x\preccurlyeq y$ implies $x+z\preccurlyeq y+z$

$x\succcurlyeq 0$ and $r\geq 0$ imply $rx\succcurlyeq 0$.

(Note: This differs from the definition of ordered linear space in note 16.)

In definitions 10 through 13, $X$ is a vector space, $(Z,\preccurlyeq )$ is an ordered vector space and $p:X\rightarrow Z$.

10.

$p$ is sublinear if $p(x+y)\preccurlyeq p(x)+p(y)$ and for all $c\in [0,\,+\infty )$, $p(cx)=cp(x)$.

11.

$p$ is convex if $p(cx+(1-c)y)\preccurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in [0,1]$.

12.

$p$ is concave if $p(cx+(1-c)y)\succcurlyeq cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in [0,1]$.

13.

$p$ is affine if $p(cx+(1-c)y)=cp(x)+(1-c)p(y)$ for all $c\in [0,1]$.

14.

Let $(\Delta ,\,\sqsubseteq )$ be a directed set and $(Z,\preccurlyeq )$ be a Dedekind complete ordered vector space. Let $B(\Delta ,\,Z)$ be the set of functions $f$ from $\Delta$ to $Z$ such that the range of $f$ has both an upper bound and a lower bound. For $f\in B(\Delta ,\,Z)$ let

$\liminf (f)=\sup _{\alpha \in \Delta }\inf _{\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta }f(\beta )$ and

$\limsup (f)=\inf _{\alpha \in \Delta }\sup _{\alpha \sqsubseteq \beta }f(\beta )$

(Since $Z$ is Dedekind complete both $\liminf (f)$ and $\limsup (f)$ exist in $Z$ and $\lim \inf (f)\preccurlyeq \limsup (f).)$ We define a $Z$-valued Banach limit on $\Delta$ to be a linear map LIM: $B(\Delta ,\,Z)\rightarrow Z$ which satisfies$$\begin{equation*} (\forall f\in B(\Delta ,\,Z)) (\liminf (f)\preccurlyeq \mathrm{LIM}\ (f)\preccurlyeq \limsup (f) \end{equation*}$$

A similarity type $\tau$ is a set $J$ of operation symbols and for each $j\in J$, an arity $I_{j}$ ($I_{j}$ indexes the argument places of $j$). An algebra of type $\tau$ is a set $A$ and for each $j\in J$, an operation $j_{A}$ from $A^{I_{j}}$ into $A$. The following is a theorem of ZF. (See Blass [1983a].)

NOTE 33

The following proof that form 99 (Rado’s selection lemma) and form 62 $(C(\infty , < \aleph _{0}))$ imply the Boolean prime ideal theorem (form 14) is due to A. Blass.

Assume Rado’s lemma and $C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0})$ and let $B$ be a Boolean algebra. Let $X=\{\{x,\overline{x}\}:x\in B\}$ where $\overline{x}$ denotes the complement of $x$ in B. For each finite subset $A$ of $X$, let $f_{A}$ be a choice function on $A$ chosen so that $\{f_{A}(Y):Y\in A\}$ can be extended to a proper ideal in the subalgebra of $B$ generated by $\bigcup A$. (Choosing $f_{A}$ for each finite $A\subseteq X$ uses $C(\infty ,\,<\aleph _{0}).)$ By Rado’s lemma there is a choice function $f$ for $X$ such that for each finite $A\subseteq X$ there is a finite $B\subseteq X$ such that $A\subseteq B$ and $f_{B}$ agrees with $f$ on $A$. Let $I=\{f(Y):Y\in X\}$. It is reasonably easy to show that $I$ is a maximal proper ideal in $B$.

NOTE 34

A proof that Alexander’s subbase lemma [14 AA] (A topological space is compact if and only if there is a subbase $S$ for the topology such that every cover by elements of $S$ has a finite subcover.) implies [14 Z] (Tychonoff’s Compactness Theorem for families of finite spaces.)

Let $\{X_{i}:i\in I\}$ be a family of non-empty finite sets and let $X=\prod _{i\in I}X_{i}$. If $X$ is empty we are done otherwise let $g\in X$ and for each $j\in I$ and $a\in X_{j}$ let $B_{j,a}=\{f\in X:f(j)\in X_{j}\backslash \{a\}\}$. $\mathcal{B} =\{B_{a,j}:j\in I$ and $a\in X_{j}\}$ is a subbase for the topology on X. We show every cover of $X$ by elements of $\mathcal{B}$ has a finite subcover. Let $\mathcal{C}$ be such a cover. If for some $j\in I,\,B_{a,j}$ and $B_{a^{\prime },j}$ are in $\mathcal{C}$ with $a\neq a^{\prime }$, then these two sets are the required finite subcover. If not then we can define an element of $X$ that is not covered by $\mathcal{C}$ as follows: $f(j)=\left\{\begin{array}{ll} a, & \mathrm{if}\ B_{j,a}\in C\\g(j), & \mathrm{otherwise} \end{array}\right. .$

NOTE 35

Form 10 $(C(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0}))$ is equivalent to [10 F] (Every $\omega$-tree has an infinite chain.) The proof that 10 implies [10 F] uses the fact that form 10 is equivalent to $UT(\aleph _{0},\,<\aleph _{0},\,\aleph _{0})$ which implies an $\omega$-tree is denumerable. For the argument that [10 F] implies form 10, let $A$ be a denumerable set of finite sets and $T$ be the set of all choice functions on initial segments of $A$. Define $<$ on $T$ by $f<g$ iff $f$ is a proper subset of $g$. $T$ is an $\omega$ tree and an infinite chain in $T$ induces a choice function on $A$. This proof is due to Arthur and Jean Rubin. A proof of the equivalence of form 10 and [10 F] also occurs in Pelc [1978].

NOTE 36

In this note we prove that form 284 (Every finitely solvable system of linear equations over a field has a solution in the field.) implies $\forall n\in \omega ,\,n\geq 2,\,C(\infty ,\,n)$ (form 61). The proof is by mathematical induction on $n$, starting with the case $n=1$ which is clear. Assume that $C(\infty ,\,k)$ is true for every $k<n$ and let $X$ be a collection of pairwise disjoint $n$ element sets. By the induction hypothesis there is a choice function $h$ for the set $Y=\{z:(\exists x\in X)(z\subseteq x)\wedge 1\leq |z|<n\}$. Let $p$ be the smallest prime that divides $n$, say $n=r\cdot p$. We define a system of linear equations over the field $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ (the integers $\mod \,p$) as follows: We have one variable $t_{a}$ for each $a\in \bigcup X$ and for each $x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}\in X$ we include the equation $t_{a_{1}}+\cdots +t_{a_{n}}=1$. This system of equations is clearly finitely satisfiable hence by form 284 it has a solution $S:\{t_{a}:a\in \bigcup \,X\}\rightarrow \mathbb{Z}_{p}$. We now define a choice function $f$ on $X$. Let $x=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}$ be an element of $X$. The solution $S$ determines a partition of $x$ into the sets $z_{m}=\{a\in x:S(t_{a})=m\},\,0\leq m\leq p-1$, some of which may be empty. However, there is no $m,\,0\leq m\leq p-1$, for which $x=z_{m}$ because the existence of such an $m$ would mean that $S(t_{a_{1}})=\cdots =S(t_{a_{n}})=m$. Hence $S(t_{a_{1}})+\cdots +S(t_{a_{n}})=m\cdot n=m\cdot (r\cdot p)=0$, which is a contradiction since $S$ is a solution to the equation $t_{a_{1}}+\cdots +t_{a_{n}}=1$.

Let $m_{0}$ be the least element of $\mathbb{Z}_{p}$ for which $z_{m_{0}}\neq \emptyset$. Since $z_{m_{0}}\neq x,\, |z_{m_{0}}|<n$ and we may therefore define $f(x)=h(z_{m_{0}})$.

NOTE 40

Notes on [94 A] and [94 B]. Brunner [1982d] proves that [94 B] implies form 13 (lemma 6, p. 164) by showing that the negation of form 13 implies the negation of [94 A] which implies the negation of [94 B]. Since [94 A] clearly implies [94 B], it only remains to prove that [94 A] implies 94 (to complete the argument for the equivalence of 94, [94 A] and [94 B]). (Form 94: $C(\aleph _{0},\,\infty ,\, \mathbb{R})$; [94 A]: The discrete topology on $\omega$ is Lindelöf; and [94 B]: There is a Lindelöf space with a closed, discrete infinite subset.)

Assume [94 A] and let $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ be a denumerable family where for all $i\in \omega ,\, A_{i}\neq \emptyset$ and $A_{i}\subseteq \mathcal{P}(\omega )$. It suffices to find a choice function for the family $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ (identifying reals with sets of natural numbers).

Now using the family $\{A_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ we define a second family of sets of sets of natural numbers $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ so that

$$\begin{equation*} \forall i\in \omega ,\, 2^{i}\in \bigcup B_{i}\ {\text{and for}}\ j\in \omega ,\,j\neq i\ {\text{implies}}\ 2^{i}\not \in \bigcup B_{j}. \tag{$\ast $} \end{equation*}$$

More specifically, for each $i\in \omega$, let $m(i)$ be the least element of $\bigcup A_{i}$. Define $f_{i}:\{k\in \omega :k\geq m(i)\}\rightarrow \omega$ by $f_{i}(k)=[2(k-m(i))+1]2^{i}$ and let $B_{i}=\{f_{i}^{\prime \prime }x:x\in A_{i}\}$. It is clear that $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}$ satisfies $(\ast )$ and that it suffices to find a choice function for $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}$. Further $\bigcup _{i\in \omega }B_{i}\cup \big \{\{k\in \omega :k\not \in \bigcup _{i\in \omega }(\bigcup \,B_{i})\}\big \}$ is an open cover for $\omega$ (using the discrete topology). Since the topology is Lindelöf there is a countable subcover $\{x_{j}:j\in \omega \}$. Defining, for each $i\in \omega ,\,F(B_{i})=x_{j}$ where $j$ is the least element of $\omega$ such that $2^{i}\in x_{j}$ provides a choice function for $\{B_{i}:i\in \omega \}$.

NOTE 41

The following proof that form 233 is true in $\mathcal{N}1$ is due to David Pincus. Form 233 is “Algebraic closures of fields, if they exist, are unique.”

(H. Läuchli has given a proof of this lemma with the additional hypothesis that the characteristic of $K$ is not equal to 2. See Jech [1973b], p. 147.)

Now let $(K,\,+,\,\cdot ,\,0,1)$ be a field in $\mathcal{N}1$ with finite support $E\subseteq A$ where $A$ is the set of atoms. Assume that $K$ is algebraically closed. We will show that every element of $K$ has support $E$. This implies that all algebraically closed fields are well orderable in $\mathcal{N}1$ and therefore the standard proof of the uniqueness of algebraic closures (using AC) is valid in $\mathcal{N}1$.

The proof is by contradiction. Assume that $x\in K$ does not have support $E$. We will arrive at a contradiction in two steps. The first is to show that for some permutation $\pi$ of $A$ which fixes $E$ pointwise, $\pi (x)\neq x$ and $\pi ^{2}$ is the identity. The permutation $\pi$ induces an automorphism of $(K,\,+,\cdot ,\,0,1)$ and we can therefore apply the lemma to conclude that $\pi (i)=-i\neq i$ for some square root $i$ of -1 in $K$. The second step is to show that for every permutation $\pi$ of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, $\pi (i)=i$ for every square root $i$ of -1 in $K$.

For step one, suppose that $x$ has support $E\cup F$ where $E\cap F=\emptyset$. Let $F^{\prime }$ be a subset of $A$ for which $|F^{\prime }|=|F|$ and $F^{\prime }\cap (E\cup F)=\emptyset$. Let $\pi$ be a permutation of $A$ which interchanges the elements of $F$ and $F^{\prime }$, that is, $\pi$ is a product of cycles of length 2, $\pi =(a_{1},\,b_{1})(a_{2},\, b_{2})\cdots (a_{n},\,b_{n})$ where $F=\{a_{1},\,\ldots ,\,a_{n}\}$ and $F^{\prime }=\{b_{1},\,\ldots ,\,b_{n}\}$. Clearly $\pi ^{2}$ is the identity and $\pi$ fixes $E$ pointwise. The proof that $\pi (x)\neq x$ is a standard permutation model argument and depends on the fact that $x$ does not have support $E$.

For step two, we note that if $i$ is a square root of –1 in K, then $i$ is a solution to the equation $x^{2}+1=0$ all of whose coefficients are fixed by any permutation that fixes $E$ pointwise. Therefore if $\eta$ is a permutation of $A$ that fixes $E$ pointwise, $\eta (i)$ is also a solution to $x^{2}+1=0$. Suppose that $i$ does not have support $E$. Let $E\cup F$ be a support of $i$ where $E\cap F=\emptyset$. By a standard permutation model argument, we can show that if $\pi$ and $\pi ^{\prime }$ are any two permutations of $A$ that fix $E$ pointwise and $\pi (F) \cap \pi ^{\prime }(F)=\emptyset$ then $\pi (x)\neq \pi ^{\prime }(x)$. It follows that the equation $x^{2}+1=0$ has infinitely many solutions in $K$ which is a contradiction and the proof is complete.

NOTE 42

In Brunner [1982a] is a study, in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ without $AC$, of conditions under which a topological space is well orderable. These conditions are summarized below.

Finally some counter examples: In the model $\mathcal{M}1$ (The basic Cohen model) $X=[0,1]$ (the closed interval in $\mathbb{R}$) with the order topology is compact, metric, separable, second countable, hereditarily Souslin and linearly ordered, but $X$ is not well orderable.

In the model $\mathcal{N}3$ (The ordered Mostowski model of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$): Let $X=[a,\,b]$ be an interval in the set of atoms with the order topology. $X$ is compact, hereditarily normal (that is $T_{5}$) and $T_{2}$. Further, each finite power of $X$ is compact, $T_{4}$ and hereditarily Souslin, but $X$ is not well orderable.

In the model $\mathcal{N}1$ (The basic Fraenkel model with a denumerable set of atoms, using the group of all permutations of the atoms and finite supports): Let $X= [A]^{<\omega }$ (all finite subsets of the set of atoms) with a basis for the topology all set of the form $\{x:E\subseteq x$ and $x\cap F=\emptyset \}$ where $E$ and $F$ range over the finite subsets of U. The space $X$ is Souslin, perfectly regular and not well orderable.

NOTE 49

In von Rimscha [1982] three transitivity conditions are considered:

$Tr.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $f$ is a function from $f$ one to one and onto $u$. This is form 175.

$Tr^{\prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $u\subseteq TC(x)$ and $f$ is a one to one function from $x$ onto $u$.

$Tr^{\prime \prime }.\ \forall x\exists u\exists f$ such that $u$ is transitive and $f$ is a one to one function from $x$ onto $u$ and $\forall s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s)$.

It is shown that in ZF, AC implies $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ and that $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ implies $Tr^{\prime }$ implies $Tr$. All proofs can be done in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ with minor modifications. It is also shown that $\mathrm{ZF} \vdash Tr\rightarrow$ form 9 (Dedekind finite $=$ finite). This could be reformulated as $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}\vdash Tr\rightarrow$ all pure Dedekind finite sets are finite. We can therefore conclude that $Tr$ (form 175) implies Dedekind finite sets of reals are finite (form 13).

It is however possible to prove in $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ that $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ (form 174) implies Dedekind finite $=$ finite (form 9). We proceed as follows: Assume $Tr^{\prime \prime }$. We first show that every infinite subset of the atoms $A$ is Dedekind infinite. Assume $B\subseteq A$ and that $B$ is infinite. We will use $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ to get a choice function for $\mathcal{P}(B)$ from which it follows that $B$ has a denumerable subset. Let $\kappa$ be the least well ordered cardinal which is not $\leq |\mathcal{P}(B)|$. For each $a\in B$ and ordinal $\alpha$, define $a_{\alpha }$ by induction: $a_{0}=a,\,a_{\lambda }=\bigcup _{\alpha <\lambda }a_{\alpha }$ for limit ordinals $\lambda$ and $a_{\alpha +1}=a_{\alpha }\cup \{a_{\alpha }\}$. $(a_{\alpha }$ is the ordinal $\alpha$ with every occurrence of $\emptyset$ replaced by $a$.) Then for each $\alpha ,\, |a_{\alpha }|=|\alpha |$. Let $B^{\prime }=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in B\}$ and let $x=\mathcal{P}(B^{\prime })$. By $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ there is a transitive set $u$ and a function $f:x\rightarrow u$ which is one to one and onto and such that for each $s\in x,\,f(s)\in TC(s)$. Suppose that $C\subseteq B$ and let $s=\{a_{\kappa }:a\in C\}\in x$. Then

$$\begin{equation*} TC(s)=\{s\}\cup s\cup \bigg (\bigcup _{a\in C}a_{\kappa }\bigg ) \end{equation*}$$

since $|TC(s)|\geq \kappa ,\,s\not \in u$. $(|u|=|\mathcal{P}(B)|$ which is not $\geq \kappa .)$. So $f(s)\in \bigcup _{a\in C}a_{\kappa }$. Since $a\neq b$ implies $a_{\kappa }\cap b_{\kappa }=\emptyset ,\, f(s)$ determines a unique element of $C$.

Now let $x$ be any infinite set. By $Tr^{\prime \prime }$ there is a transitive $u$ and a one to one function $f$ from $x$ onto $u$. If $u$ contains only finitely many atoms, then the von Rimscha proof can be modified to show that $x$ has a denumerable subset. If $u$ contains an infinite set of atoms $B$, then by the first argument $B$ and therefore $x$ contains a denumerable subset.

Problem (from von Rimscha [1982]): Are any of the implications $Tr\rightarrow Tr^{\prime }\rightarrow Tr^{\prime \prime }\rightarrow AC$ provable in ZF?

Definitions from Andreka/Nemeti [1981] and Höft/Howard [1981].

An algebra is a pair $(A,\,F)$ where $A$ is a set and $F$ is a function from an index set $I$ such that for each $i\in I$, there is a $k_{i}\in \omega$ such that $F(i)$ is a function from $A^{k_{i}}$ into $A$. The function $\Delta$ with domain $I$ defined by $\Delta (i)=k_{i}$ is called the type of the algebra $(A,\,F)$. Two algebras of the same type are similar.

3.

ZF + $\Omega =\omega _{\alpha +1}$, for any $\alpha$.

In fact, item 1 holds in $\mathcal{M}17$ itself. It is clear that ZFC $\vdash \Omega =\omega _{1}$ (form 315).

In Gitik [1985], the following theorem is given: Suppose $M$ is a countable model of ZFC and $\kappa$ is an almost huge cardinal in $M$. (See note 20 for the definition of various types of inaccessible cardinals.) If $S$ is any subset of $\kappa$ consisting of nonlimit cardinals, then there is a model $\mathcal{M}(S)$ of ZF such that the regular cardinals are exactly $\{\aleph _{\alpha }:\alpha \in S\cup \{0\}\}$. In the case that $S=\emptyset$, then all uncountable $\aleph _{\alpha }$’s are singular. Note, however, that in $\mathcal{M}17$ all uncountable $\aleph _{\alpha }$’s are singular. Further, the construction of $\mathcal{M}17$ requires only the existence of a strongly compact cardinal which is weaker than the existence of an almost huge cardinal.

NOTE 57

Truss [1995] studies the various structures an amorphous set can carry. (A set is amorphous if it is infinite but is not the disjoint union of two infinite sets.) If $\pi$ is a partition of an amorphous set $U$ into infinitely many parts, then each part must be finite. (Otherwise, if $X$ were an infinite part, then $U=X\cup (U-X)$, contradicting the fact that $U$ is amorphous.) Define a map $f$ from $U$ into $\omega$ such that for each $x\in U,\,f(x)=n$ where $x\in \xi \in \pi$ and $|\xi |=n$. Since $U$ is amorphous, the range of $f$ must be finite. Since $U=\bigcup \{f^{-1}(n): n\in$ range of $f$}, there is a unique $n$ such that $f^{-1}(n)$ is infinite. Let $n(\pi )$ be this unique $n$, then $\{\xi \in \pi :|\xi |=n(\pi )\}$ is infinite.

Let $\Pi (U)$ be the set of finitary partitions of $U$ and let $n(U)= \sup \{n(\pi ):\pi \in \Pi (U)\}$. If $n(U)$ is finite, $U$ is called bounded, and if $n(U)$ infinite, $U$ is called unbounded.

J. L. Hickman [1979b] shows that if $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ are Dedekind finite cardinals then the following are equivalent: (1) lub$\{\Gamma ,\,\Delta \}$ exists, (2) $\Gamma$ and $\Delta$ are comparable and (3) gib $\{\Gamma ,\,\Delta \}$ exists.

NOTE 59

Form 191 is the statement: There is a set $S$ such that for every set $a$, there is an ordinal $\alpha$ and a function from $S\times \alpha$ onto $a$ and form 182 is: There is an aleph whose cofinality is greater than $\aleph _{0}$. In Blass [1979] it is proved, assuming form 191, that $\forall A$ there is a limit ordinal $\alpha$ such that $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\alpha$. If $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\alpha$, then $A$ cannot be mapped cofinally onto $\aleph _{\alpha }$. Therefore form 191 implies form 182.

Blass also shows that if 191 holds with a set $S$ then form 14 (the Boolean Prime Ideal Theorem) holds if and only if there is an ultrafilter $U$ on $S^{<\omega }$ that is regular in the sense that $\{p\in S^{<\omega }: s\in$ range $p\}$ is in $U$ for every $s\in S$.

With regard to $(191,n)$, Blass shows that 191 holds in most known models of $\mathrm{ZF}^{0}$ or ZF. In particular,

1.

Every permutation model whose class of atoms forms a set satisfies 191.

2.

Every symmetric model satisfies 191. (A symmetric model is a model constructed from a ground model $M$ of ZFC by taking a complete Boolean algebra $B$ in $M$, an $M$ generic filter $G$ in $B$, a group $\mathcal{G}$ of automorphisms of $B$ and a normal filter of subgroups of $\mathcal{G}$. The model consists of members of $M[G]$ that have hereditarily symmetric names.)

3.

If $V$ is any model of ZFC and $A\in V$, then the submodel $HOD(A)$ of sets hereditarily ordinal definable over A satisfies 191.

NOTE 61

Kanovei [1979] studies the relationships between $AC(K)$ and $DC(K)$ where $K$ is either in the analytic or projective hierarchy. We give definitions and summarize some of the results from Kanovei [1979]. $AC(K)$ is: For any $P\subseteq \omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega$ with domain $\omega$, if $P\in K$, then there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle$ of elements of ${^{\omega }}\omega$ with $\langle k,\,x_{k}\rangle \in P$ for all $k\in \omega$. And

$DC(K)$ is: For every $P\subseteq {^{\omega }}\omega \times {^{\omega }}\omega$ with domain $^{\omega }\omega$, if $P\in K$ then for any $y\in {^{\omega }}\omega$ there is a sequence $\langle x_{k}: k\in \omega \rangle$ with $x_{0}=y$ and for all $k\in \omega , \langle x_{k},\,x_{k+1}\rangle \in P$. The sets in the analytic hierarchy $(\varSigma _{n}^{1},\, \varPi _{n}^{1}$ and $\varDelta _{n}^{1}$ for $n\in \omega )$ and the sets in the projective hierarchy $(\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{n}^{1},\, \boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1}$ and $\boldsymbol{\Delta }_{n}^{1}$ for $n\in \omega )$ are defined as follows: For purposes of these definitions $^{k,\ell }\omega$ is ${^{k}}\omega \times {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega )$ and a relation $R\subseteq {^{k,\ell }}\omega$ is of rank $(k,\,\ell )$.

1.

$R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell )$ is arithmetic if for all $\mathbf{m}\in {^{k}} \omega$ and all $\boldsymbol{\alpha }\in {^{\ell }}(^{\omega }\omega )$, $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha })$ iff $Q_{1}x_{1}\ldots Q_{r}x_{r}P(\mathbf{x},\,\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },)$ where $P\subseteq ^{r+k,\ell }\omega$ is recursive, and each $Q_{i}$ is either $\exists$ or $\forall$.

2.

$R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell )$ is analytic if $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha })$ iff $Q_{1}\beta _{1}\ldots Q_{r}\beta _{r}P(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\beta _{1},\,\ldots ,\,\beta _{r})$ where $P$ is of rank $(k,\,\ell +r)$ and is arithmetic.

3.

(The analytic hierarchy)

(i)

$\varSigma _{0}^{1}=\varPi _{0}^{1}=$ the arithmetic relations.

(ii)

$\varSigma _{r+1}^{1}=\{\exists \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P$ has rank $(k,\, \ell +1)\}$

(ii)

$\varPi _{n+1}^{1}=\{\forall \beta P(\mathbf{m},\,\beta ,\,\boldsymbol{\alpha }):P\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}\wedge P$ has rank $(k,\, \ell +1)\}$

(iv)

$\varDelta _{r}^{1}=\varSigma _{r}^{1}\cap \varPi _{r}^{1}$.

4.

$R$ of rank $(k,\,\ell )$ is recursive in $\boldsymbol{\beta }$ iff the characteristic function $K_{R}(\mathbf{m},\, \boldsymbol{\alpha })$ of $R$ is $G(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta })$ for some partial recursive $G$.

5.

Assume $\boldsymbol{\beta }$ has rank $(0,\,\ell )$ then $\varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ]$ and $\varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }]$ are defined by $R\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }]$ iff $R(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha })\leftrightarrow S(\mathbf{m},\,\boldsymbol{\alpha },\,\boldsymbol{\beta })$ for some $S\in \varSigma _{r}^{1}$. $\varPi _{r}^{1}[\boldsymbol{\beta }]$ is defined similarly.

6.

(The projective hierarchy)

(i)

$\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varSigma _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}$

(ii)

$\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{r}^{1}=\bigcup \{\varPi _{r}^{1}[\beta ]:b\in {^{\omega }}\omega \}$

(iii)

$\boldsymbol{\Delta }_{r}^{1}=\boldsymbol{\Sigma }_{r}^{1}\cap \boldsymbol{\Pi } 1_{r}$.

In Kanovei [1979], it is shown for any $n\geq 2$ that, $AC(\varPi _{n+1}^{1})$ does not follow, in ZF from $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1})$, that $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1})$ implies $AC(\varPi _{n}^{1})$ and that $AC(\varPi _{n}^{1})$ does not imply $DC(\boldsymbol{\Pi }_{n}^{1})$. Kanovei [1976] has further results on $AC$ and the projective hierarchy. See forms [0 X], 194 and 199.

Form 200 is studied in Dawson/Howard [1976] where it is shown that

1.

Each of

(a)

$\exists$ infinite $x$ such that $2^{x}<x!$

(b)

$\exists$ infinite $x$ such that $2^{x}>x!$ and

(c)

are consistent with ZF. ($x!$ is the cardinality of the set of all one to one functions from $x$ onto $x$.).

2.

for all $x,\,2x=x$ implies $2^{x}\leq x!$.

In Pincus [1978] a model of ZF is constructed in which AC (form 1) is false, $\forall$ infinite $x,\, 2x=x$ (form 3) is false and $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=x!$ is true. Also true in this mod el are $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}|$ and $\forall$ infinite $x,\,2^{x}=|x^{x}-x!|$.
